GPU slice_sample(): indices drawn in R, rows gathered on the GPU

Source: R/slice.R
slice_sample_native.Rd

Reproduces dplyr's own RNG stream bit-for-bit by generating row indices on the CPU with the exact same sample.int() call sequence real dplyr makes, then gathering those indices on the GPU via the existing gpu_slice_indices() primitive – there is no AST node for slice_sample() at all, unlike every other verb in this package: the index vector is the whole point (it must be generated on the CPU to consume R's global RNG state the same way real dplyr does), so there is nothing left for a lazy AST/optimizer to defer.

Usage

slice_sample_native(.data, gm, amount, is_prop, replace, fallback)

Arguments

.data

A tbl_gpu object. Pending lazy ops are computed first: the CPU-side index generation needs a real row count/grouping, which a lazy AST doesn't have.

gm

A list(mode, group_cols) as returned by slice_group_mode()

amount, is_prop

As resolved by resolve_slice_amount()

replace

Logical scalar, slice_sample()'s own replace=

fallback

function(tbl) running dplyr's slice_sample() on the CPU. Used when a group is empty and replace = TRUE still asks for rows: sample.int(0, size, replace = TRUE) fails, and dplyr raises that from slice(), after drawing the groups before it, so dplyr runs it.

Value

A new (always eager) tbl_gpu, or fallback()'s result

Details

Semantics checked against dplyr 1.2.1 (dplyr:::slice_sample.data.frame, dplyr:::sample_int, dplyr:::get_slice_size, dplyr:::compute_by_groups):

  • Ungrouped: exactly one sample.int(nrow, size, replace = replace) call (dplyr:::sample_int's own body: if (size == 0L) integer(0) else sample.int(n, size, prob = wt, replace = replace), wt always NULL here since weight_by= never reaches this function – see below).

  • group_by()-grouped: dplyr iterates groups in ascending group-key order (NA-key group last) – the same order dplyr::group_by() itself produces (taken from dplyr::group_by()/dplyr::group_rows() on the collected group columns, so it can't drift from dplyr's ordering). One sample.int() call per group, in that order, consuming the RNG stream in that same order; the resulting rows are concatenated in the same (group-key) order, as dplyr's output is: a reordering relative to input row order, as for the other grouped slice_*() verbs. Output stays grouped by the same columns.

  • by=: dplyr's own compute_by_groups() groups via vctrs::vec_group_loc(), which orders groups by first-appearance position in the input, not ascending group-key order: the RNG draw order and the output row order both follow first-appearance order (not ascending key, and not a final sort by original row position either), as for summarise(.by=) and the grouped slice() desugar. Implemented with vctrs::vec_group_loc() directly (the function compute_by_groups() itself calls), so the group order can't diverge. Output is always ungrouped, as by= always is.

  • n=/prop= resolution: see compute_slice_sample_size()'s own docs for the exact (and slightly asymmetric) replace=-dependent clamp rule, checked against dplyr:::get_slice_size()'s source. Oversampling n without replace does not error – it silently clamps to the table's (or group's) own row count, same as slice_head()/slice_tail().

  • weight_by= always falls back to CPU (see slice_sample.tbl_gpu()) – gpu_fallback() re-runs the real dplyr::slice_sample() call, which already reproduces the identical sample.int(..., prob = wt) behavior, so there is nothing to gain (and real complexity to lose, since wt needs the actual data values, not just group columns) from a native path for this case.
